n: Jesus was born in Bethlehem during the reign of Herod the Great, who died about 4 BC. Wise men from the east — likely Persia or Babylonia — arrived in Jerusalem seeking Him.

f.g: Herod the Great, appointed king of Judea by Rome; infamous for cruelty.
Greek magoi — scholars of the stars from the east, perhaps Persian priests or astronomers.

n: They ask, “Where is the one born King of the Jews? We saw His star rise and came to worship Him.” Samuel the Lamanite also prophesied a new star at Christ’s birth.

f.g: JST reads “Where is the child that is born, the Messiah of the Jews?”

n: King Herod was alarmed, and all Jerusalem with him. Herod jealously guarded his throne and had executed even his own family members.
Herod gathered the chief priests and scribes and asked where the Messiah was to be born. The religious experts knew the answer from scripture.

f.g: Experts in copying and interpreting the law of Moses.

n: They answered: in Bethlehem of Judea, as the prophet wrote.
They quote Micah: from little Bethlehem will come a ruler who will shepherd God’s people Israel. Matthew blends Micah’s words with God’s promise to David to “feed my people.”
Herod secretly called the wise men and carefully found out when the star first appeared, already plotting.
He sent them to Bethlehem: “Find the child and report back, so I can worship Him too.” His “worship” was a lie to cover murder.

f.w: that I may come and worship him also
f.g: A deceptive pretext; his real aim appears in verse 16.

n: The star led them on to the place where the young child was. God guided seekers from afar.

f.w: stood over where the young child was
f.g: The star marked the exact location.

n: When they saw the star again, they were overjoyed — Matthew piles up words to show their joy.

Entering the house, they found the young child with Mary, bowed down, and worshiped Him. They gave gold (for a king), frankincense (for worship of God), and myrrh (for burial), gifts often seen as symbols of who He is.

f.g: By now the family lived in a house; Jesus was a “young child,” perhaps up to two years old.
A fragrant resin burned as incense in worship.
A costly resin used in perfumes and burial.

n: Warned by God in a dream not to return to Herod, they went home another way.

f.w: warned of God in a dream

n: Once they left, an angel told Joseph in a dream to flee to Egypt with the child and Mary, because Herod wanted to kill Him. Egypt had long been a refuge for Israelites.
Joseph got up that very night and fled with them to Egypt. His prompt obedience saved the Savior’s life.
They stayed there until Herod died. Matthew sees Hosea’s words fulfilled: “Out of Egypt have I called my son.” As Israel was God’s son brought out of Egypt, so Jesus relives Israel’s story.

f.w: Out of Egypt have I called my son

n: Furious at being outwitted, Herod ordered all boys two and under in and around Bethlehem killed. Bethlehem was a small village, so perhaps a few dozen children died — a tragedy typical of Herod’s brutality.
This fulfilled words of Jeremiah.
Rachel, Israel’s ancestral mother buried near Bethlehem, is pictured weeping for her lost children. Jeremiah’s original verse is followed by a promise of hope and return.

f.g: Ramah, a town north of Jerusalem where exiles gathered.

n: After Herod died, an angel again appeared to Joseph in a dream in Egypt.
“Get up and take the child and His mother back to Israel; those who sought His life are dead.” The words echo God’s command to Moses to return to Egypt.

f.w: they are dead which sought the young child's life

n: Joseph obeyed and returned with them to the land of Israel.
But Herod’s son Archelaus was ruling Judea, and Joseph feared him. Warned in another dream, he went to Galilee instead. Archelaus was so harsh that Rome removed him in AD 6.

f.g: Son of Herod the Great, ruler of Judea from 4 BC to AD 6.

n: They settled in Nazareth, a small, unimportant village. Matthew says this fulfilled “He shall be called a Nazarene” — perhaps a wordplay on the Hebrew netzer, “branch,” a messianic title.

f.g: Possibly linked to netzer (“Branch”) in Isaiah 11:1.
